content: Infantile colic is characterized by intense crying episodes lasting at least three hours per day, occurring on at least three days per week, for a minimum of three weeks. This condition affects a significant number of infants and their families globally. While the symptoms are broad and nonspecific, they are not typically indicative of a disease. However, in a small subset of infants, these symptoms may signal an underlying medical condition that requires further evaluation. Probiotics are live microorganisms that can modify the host's gut microbiota and confer health benefits. Commonly used probiotics include strains from the genera Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Streptococcus. Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiota of infants with colic differs from that of healthy infants. Probiotics are hypothesized to restore this imbalance, potentially promoting a healthier intestinal environment. Given their low cost and widespread availability, probiotics are being explored as a preventive measure to reduce the incidence and severity of infantile colic. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of using probiotics prophylactically to prevent or mitigate the severity of infantile colic. A comprehensive search was conducted in January 2018 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, as well as trial registries. Additional efforts included handsearching abstracts from relevant meetings, reviewing reference lists, conducting citation searches, and contacting authors, experts, and probiotic manufacturers to identify unpublished studies. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving newborns under one month of age who had not been diagnosed with infantile colic at the time of recruitment. Studies comparing any probiotic (alone or in combination with a prebiotic, referred to as synbiotics) to no intervention, placebo, or other interventions were included, provided the primary focus was on the impact of the intervention on infantile colic. The review identified 3284 records, of which 21 were selected for full-text review. Ultimately, six studies involving 1886 participants met the inclusion criteria. These studies compared probiotics to placebo. Two studies investigated Lactobacillus reuteri DSM, two examined multi-strain probiotics, one focused on Lactobacillus rhamnosus, and one studied a combination of Lactobacillus paracasei and Bifidobacterium animalis. In two studies, probiotics were administered during pregnancy and continued postnatally. The risk of bias for randomization was deemed low across all six trials. Allocation concealment was rated as low in two studies and unclear in four. All studies were blinded and exhibited low risk for attrition and reporting bias. A random-effects meta-analysis of three studies (1148 participants) found no significant difference between the probiotic and placebo groups in the occurrence of new cases of colic (risk ratio [RR] 0.46, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.18 to 1.19; low-certainty evidence; I² = 72%). Similarly, a meta-analysis of all six studies (1851 participants) found no significant difference in the occurrence of serious adverse events (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.14 to 7.21; low-certainty evidence). Serious adverse events included meconium plug obstruction, patent ductus arteriosus, and neonatal hepatitis, with only four events reported across all studies. A random-effects meta-analysis of three studies (707 participants) demonstrated a reduction in daily crying time by an average of 32.57 minutes (95% CI –55.60 to –9.54; low-certainty evidence; I² = 93%) in favor of probiotics. Subgroup analysis of Lactobacillus reuteri, the most studied probiotic, showed a reduction in daily crying time by 44.26 minutes (95% CI –66.6 to –21.9; I² = 92%) compared to placebo. In conclusion, there is no definitive evidence to suggest that probiotics are more effective than placebo in preventing infantile colic. However, probiotic use was associated with a reduction in daily crying time compared to placebo. No significant differences in adverse effects were observed between the groups. The certainty of the evidence was rated as low across all outcomes, limiting the confidence in these findings and leaving open the possibility that further research could alter these results.
